processing: Fully oxidised black tea from Yunnan leaf, rolled into tight spirals in the manner of green Bi Luo Chun. One documented lot is pure bud; others may include leaf.
harvest_season: Spring; some makers use only first-flush buds, others one bud with one leaf.
appearance_dry: Tight, small spirals of dark leaf and downy golden tips.
appearance_wet: Spirals open slowly into soft reddish-brown buds and small leaves.
taste_profile: Malty and sweet, with hints of sugarcane and milk chocolate and a light floral note.

brewing.notes: Tight spirals open slowly, so the second steep often has more to say than the first. Bud-heavy lots prefer water a little off the boil.

vintage_note: Sold by the year's harvest, usually spring, as with most fine Dian Hong, and best drunk within a couple of years. Check the label: Yunnan Bi Luo Chun also exists as a green tea, so the name alone doesn't tell you what's in the bag.
description:
This is a black tea that borrows a green tea's name. The name here points to the shape, a small snail-like spiral, and not to Jiangsu's famous green.

The leaf is Yunnan material, fully oxidised and rolled tight. It looks much like Dian Hong Jin Luo, another spiral-rolled Yunnan black tea.

Expect a strong but smooth cup, with sugarcane, malt and chocolate in the notes people give. Bud-rich leaf turns on you if you leave it in the pot, so keep steeps short.

When buying, check the word 'black' or 'hong': a green Yunnan Bi Luo Chun made in Ning'er County exists too, and listings can be confusing. Ask whether the lot is pure bud, since that changes both price and cup.
history: Little is documented about who first made it or when. It appears to be a recent idea from Yunnan's black tea makers, trading on the fame of the Jiangsu green; the sellers who offer it name the Simao area, and no older record of the name was found.
